1992 promises to be a
year of progress and opportunit)' for Psi
Upsilon.
Now each alumnus has the opportunity to support the Psi
Upsilon Fraternity and the Psi Upsilon Foundation alike through
the Foundation's new Annual Fund. The Foundation's Annual
Fund will replace the Fraternity's Annual Giving Program and
any gifts made to tiie Psi Upsilon Foundation Annual Fund will
be fully ttix-deductible.
With the retirement of Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39, as Execu
tive Director of the Psi Upsilon Foundation, the Foundation's
administrative expenses will be significantly reduced as the dayto-day operation will be handled by Mark A. 'Williams, Phi '76,
Executive Director of the Fraternity. Accordingly, an even
greater portion of your contribution to Psi Upsilon v\all reach our
undergraduate brothers in the form of educational programs.
The Foundation will begin to position itself as a
key player in
the frateruit\ world, and will increase its ability to carry out its
original puiposes. The Psi Upsilon Foundation was formed to do
the following:
� to
provide financial assistance through undergraduate schol
arships;
to provide educational reference material and equipment;
to
promote programs which encourage scholarship, charac
ter and moralit\', including programs of visitation and coun
seling;
� and to support the creation of presentation material of an
intellectual interest.
In keeping with this role, the Foundation will provide seed
nu)ne\- to the Fraternity for the development of an innovative
educational program built around values and ethics at the chapter
leN-el.
The Fraternity will also begin 1992 1)\' installing its forty-first
chapter, the Beta Alpha, at Miami University, Oxford, Ohio. Psi
Upsilon will continue to explore opportunities for expansion at
excellent colleges and universities in the United States and Can
ada.
The 1992 Convention will be the first one held in Canada in
a decade and will find Psi U's gathering in Toronto this summer.
Look for a different format at this year's Annual Convention.
Those attending will find educational programs for chapter leaders and for alumni, as well as
joint activities. The 1992 Conven
tion, the 149th, promises to be a
singular event in our
Fraternity's
illustrious histoiy.
The 199()'s have to be a decade of progress for Psi Upsilon.
Fraternities are under attack for reasons which would have been
difficult for our Founders to understand. The right to freely associ
ate is (juestioned, if not entirely condemned on some
campuses.
Faculties and administrators demand the right to choose a frater
nity's members or even in.sist that fraternities should not exist
because they are anti-intellectual, racist, sexist clubs which pro
mote only a hedonistic value system.
Of course, those of us who have worked with Psi Upsilon over
the past two decades know that this is by and large bunk; that
the public image of fraternities lias been spoiled by a decade of
isolated, but highlv visible, hazing and drinking incidents which
have resulted in a
plethora of lawsuits and barely affordable
insurance premiums.
Your Fraternity has responded to this with a
comprehensive
risk management program which de-emphasizes alcohol use and
encourages constructive educational programs at the chapter
level to replace pledge activities which have been permeated,
unfortunately, by elements which are antithetical to the concept
of brotherhood and fraternity membership. This program will be
one ofthe bulwarks of Psi Upsilon during the 90's.
1992 will also see further refinements in Psi Upsilon's member
ship development program, as well as further contributions to
the growth of college fraternities in our two nations.
Psi Upsilon knows that it can count on all of its members to
help with the crucial work ahead.
Yours in the bonds.
Charles M. Hall, Nu Alpha '71

(Washington, DC) As Director of the

collected. Exclaiming, "You threw away

Brother Webster as a
gift when he was
made the head of the FBI. It once
again

in the attic.

LET YOUR HOOVES DO
THE WALKING
(Urbana, IL) As a
part of an innovative
new
recycling program, cattle at the Uni
versity of Illinois are
sleeping on old tele
phone books instead of hay. The university
is able to buy the low-grade paper for less
than the hay and the animals seem to pre
fer the paper. After the animals have re
duced the paper to
pulp by sitting, walk
ing, and sleeping on it, the paper is
removed for recycling and fresh paper
takes it place. And thus the cycle is re
peated.
UNDERAGE DRINKING
STILL A PROBLEM
(Washington, DC) Three quarters of
the public believes that teenage drinking
is a
bigger problem now than five years ago
according to nationwide survey of adults
commissioned by the Century Council.
"Small wonder: the enforcement of under
age drinking laws has been so riddled with
loopholes, lip service, and laxity," Surgeon
General Antonia C. Novello reported,
"that the law was a
myth.'" She holds just
about everyone accountable�
teenagers,
parents, law enforcement officials, judges,
and retailers. Her surveys estimate that
40% of the nations 20 million junior and
senior high school students drink weekly.
Nearly 7 million students buy their booze
the "easy" way
�
they walk into a store and
buy it. Another survey this year by the
Insurance Institute for Highway Safety
found that 99 out of 100 retail outlets in
the District of Columbia sold beer to un
derage males without asking them to show
identification.
"You could throw all the resources in
the world into enforcement, but you're
missing the point," said Tom Goodale,
Vice President for Student Affairs at Vir
ginia Tech. "By making drinking illegal un
der the age of 21, we have glorified the
ritual, put it on a
pedestal."
